title: FHA 203(k) Standard vs Limited: Which One Fits?
metaDescription: Standard vs Limited FHA 203(k) loans: the $75,000 Limited cap, $5,000 Standard minimum, $15,000 inspection threshold, consultant role and eligible repairs.
h1: FHA 203(k) Standard vs Limited: How the Two Programs Differ
dek: The Limited 203(k) covers nonstructural repairs up to $75,000 in rehabilitation costs, with a consultant optional. The Standard 203(k) covers structural work and larger projects, requires at least $5,000 in rehabilitation costs, and always requires an FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant.
keyTakeaways: Both versions let an eligible buyer or homeowner finance the purchase or refinance and the renovation in one FHA-insured mortgage.
The Limited 203(k) is for minor remodeling and nonstructural repairs with rehabilitation costs up to $75,000.
The Standard 203(k) is for structural work, major remodeling, additions and projects above the Limited cap, with rehabilitation costs of at least $5,000.
A 203(k) Consultant is required on every Standard 203(k) and optional on a Limited 203(k), although the lender may require one.
Luxury items such as new pools, spas and outdoor kitchens are not eligible, and most lenders do not allow borrowers to do the work themselves.

sections.body:
An FHA 203(k) loan is a mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration that lets an eligible homebuyer or homeowner finance both the property and the cost of repairs or renovations in a single loan. It can be used with a purchase or with a refinance.

Without the program, a buyer who finds a house that needs work faces a difficult sequence: qualify for a mortgage on a house that may not meet lending standards in its current condition, close, then find separate cash or a second loan to pay for repairs. The 203(k) combines those steps. The lender bases the loan on the value the home is expected to have after the work is done, and the renovation money is held and paid out as work is completed.

The program exists to expand homeownership and help revitalize existing housing. It opens up homes that would otherwise appeal only to cash buyers and investors: houses with dated kitchens and baths, worn-out systems, deferred maintenance or damage that conventional financing will not touch.

The 203(k) is an owner-occupant program. It can be used on eligible one- to four-unit properties, but the borrower must occupy one of the units. It is not a tool for investors buying rentals, although real estate agents who work with investors often encounter it when an owner-occupant buyer is competing for the same distressed property.

There are two versions, the Standard 203(k) and the Limited 203(k). They share the same basic idea but differ in what work they cover, how much renovation they allow and how much oversight they require.

The Limited 203(k) is designed for minor remodeling and nonstructural repairs. Total rehabilitation costs can be up to $75,000.

Typical Limited 203(k) work includes the kinds of improvements that make an older or dated house comfortable, safe and current without changing its structure:
- Kitchen and bathroom remodeling that does not move structural walls.
- New flooring, interior and exterior painting, and drywall repair.
- Roof replacement and gutter work.
- Furnace, boiler, air conditioning and water heater replacement.
- Plumbing and electrical repairs and upgrades.
- Window and door replacement.
- Weatherization and energy improvements such as insulation.
- Accessibility improvements.
- Repair of existing features such as a deck, porch or pool.

Inspection rules depend on the size of the project. For Limited 203(k) projects over $15,000, an inspection is required. For projects of $15,000 or less, the lender may decide whether an inspection is necessary.

A 203(k) Consultant is optional on a Limited 203(k), though the lender may require one. In practice that means the contractor's bid and the lender's review carry more of the weight in defining the work, which is why a clear, itemized contractor proposal matters so much on a Limited loan.

The Limited 203(k) is generally meant for projects that let the household live in the home, or move in soon, without a long period of displacement. It is a lighter-weight process than the Standard version, with less paperwork and simpler oversight, which makes it attractive for buyers whose houses need real work but not major reconstruction.

The Standard 203(k) is designed for major rehabilitation, structural work and more complex renovation projects. Rehabilitation costs must total at least $5,000, and an FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant is required.

Work that typically calls for a Standard 203(k) includes:
- Structural alterations, such as removing or relocating load-bearing walls.
- Foundation repair or replacement.
- Major remodeling that reconfigures kitchens, baths or living space.
- Room additions.
- Certain conversions of one- to four-unit properties, such as changing the number of units within program limits.
- Extensive repairs to houses that have been vacant, damaged or neglected.
- Any project where rehabilitation costs exceed the $75,000 Limited 203(k) cap.

When a project goes above the Limited cap, the Standard 203(k) can be used, subject to applicable FHA mortgage limits and other program requirements. The overall loan is still bound by the FHA loan limit for the county and by the borrower's ability to qualify.

The Standard version carries more structure. The consultant inspects the property, prepares a detailed write-up of the required and requested work with a cost estimate, reviews contractor bids against it, and inspects the work before each draw is released. Change orders go through the consultant and the lender. A contingency reserve is typically built into the loan to cover unforeseen conditions.

That structure adds steps and time compared to a Limited loan, but it is what allows the program to finance serious renovation safely. For houses with structural problems or for buyers planning a significant transformation, the Standard 203(k) is the version designed for the job.

sections.h2: Standard vs Limited 203(k): the key differences side by side
sections.body:
The two programs differ in five main ways.

Scope of work:
- Limited: minor remodeling and nonstructural repairs.
- Standard: major rehabilitation, structural work, additions and complex projects.

Rehabilitation cost:
- Limited: up to $75,000 in total rehabilitation costs.
- Standard: at least $5,000 in rehabilitation costs, and it can be used above the Limited cap, subject to FHA mortgage limits and program requirements.

203(k) Consultant:
- Limited: optional, though the lender may require one.
- Standard: required on every loan.

Inspections:
- Limited: required for projects over $15,000; at $15,000 or less, the lender decides whether an inspection is necessary.
- Standard: the consultant performs inspections throughout the project, including before draws are released.

Process and paperwork:
- Limited: a lighter process with less documentation and simpler disbursement of funds.
- Standard: a more detailed process with a consultant's write-up, draw inspections and formal change order approvals.

A simple way to decide: if the work touches the structure of the house, adds space, converts units, or the rehabilitation budget is above $75,000, you are almost certainly looking at a Standard 203(k). If the work is cosmetic and system-level, such as kitchens, baths, flooring, roof, HVAC and windows, and the budget fits under the cap, the Limited 203(k) is usually simpler and quicker.

Your lender makes the final determination based on the property, the proposed work and current program rules, so the decision should be made together with an FHA-approved lender early in the process.

A 203(k) Consultant is an independent professional approved by FHA to help define, document and oversee 203(k) renovations. The consultant works for the integrity of the project, not for the contractor.

On a Standard 203(k), where a consultant is required, the consultant typically:
- Inspects the property before the loan is finalized and identifies required repairs, including health and safety items and items needed to meet FHA property standards.
- Prepares a detailed work write-up describing each repair and improvement, along with a cost estimate.
- Reviews contractor bids against the write-up so the lender can confirm costs are reasonable and complete.
- Inspects the work at each draw request and confirms which items are complete before the lender releases funds.
- Reviews and documents change orders when the scope changes.
- Performs a final inspection when the work is done.

On a Limited 203(k), a consultant is optional unless the lender requires one. Some borrowers and lenders choose to use one anyway, especially on older homes or projects near the top of the Limited range, because the consultant's write-up and inspections reduce the chance of surprises.

For a contractor, the consultant's write-up is the scope. Bids should follow its items and its order so the lender and consultant can match each price to each task. Contractors who are used to 203(k) work price directly against the write-up and expect each draw to be checked against completed items.

sections.h2: What work is eligible, and what is not?
sections.body:
Most repairs and renovations to the home are eligible under the 203(k) program. Eligible improvements commonly include:
- Roofs, gutters and downspouts.
- Plumbing, electrical and HVAC systems.
- Kitchens and bathrooms.
- Flooring, painting, drywall and trim.
- Windows, doors and siding.
- Energy efficiency and weatherization improvements.
- Accessibility improvements for people with disabilities.
- Health and safety corrections, including lead-based paint hazard reduction.
- Repairs to existing features, including pool repairs.
- On the Standard 203(k): structural repairs, foundation work, additions and certain unit conversions.

Work that is not eligible includes luxury additions such as new pools, spas and outdoor kitchens. Items the program considers luxuries rather than improvements to the livability, safety or value of the home are generally excluded.

Who does the work also matters. Most lenders do not allow buyers to perform the renovations themselves. The program expects the work to be completed by qualified contractors who provide bids, are paid through the draw process and stand behind the work.

Occupancy rules apply as well. The borrower must occupy the home, and for two- to four-unit properties, the borrower must occupy one of the units. Depending on the project, renovations may be completed before or after moving in, and the lender will consider whether the home is livable during the work.

Because program details can change, confirm eligibility for any specific item with your lender before finalizing the scope.

sections.h2: Which houses fit a Limited 203(k), and which need a Standard?
sections.body:
Looking at real houses makes the choice clearer.

A solid but dated ranch or split-level with an original kitchen, worn carpet, an old furnace and a roof near the end of its life is a classic Limited 203(k). The structure is sound, the work is system and finish replacement, and the household can usually move in during or soon after the work.

A mid-century house with a roof, windows and a bathroom that need replacing, plus some electrical upgrades, also fits the Limited program as long as the total stays under the cap and no walls move.

A pre-war house with a settling foundation, sagging floor framing and a kitchen the buyer wants opened to the dining room needs a Standard 203(k). Foundation work and removing a load-bearing wall are structural.

A vacant house with freeze-damaged plumbing, water damage, missing fixtures and a failing roof may technically be repaired with nonstructural work, but the size and uncertainty of the project often push it to the Standard program, where the consultant's write-up and contingency reserve help manage unknowns.

A two-flat or duplex where the buyer plans to live in one unit and rent the other can use either version, depending on the work. Converting a property's unit count is a Standard 203(k) project.

A house where the buyer wants to add a bedroom or a second story needs a Standard 203(k), because additions are structural.

When in doubt, the deciding questions are whether the work is structural and whether the total stays under $75,000.

sections.h2: Who the 203(k) fits, and how to get started
sections.body:
The 203(k) program fits several groups well.

Homebuyers who want to live in a neighborhood where move-in-ready homes are scarce or priced beyond reach can consider houses that need repairs, financing purchase and renovation in one mortgage. That expands the range of homes they can consider.

Homeowners who want to renovate can use a 203(k) refinance to fund repairs and improvements through their mortgage.

Real estate agents can help buyers consider properties that need repairs rather than limiting the search to move-in-ready inventory, which is especially useful in tight markets.

Lenders benefit from working with experienced renovation contractors who can develop detailed scopes and estimates and complete work through the 203(k) process, including draw inspections and documentation.

The usual starting sequence:
- Talk with an FHA-approved lender that originates 203(k) loans to confirm eligibility and which version fits.
- Find a property and, for a Standard loan, engage a 203(k) Consultant to inspect it and prepare the write-up.
- Get detailed, itemized bids from qualified contractors that match the write-up or proposed scope.
- Let the lender order the appraisal based on the as-completed value and finalize the loan.
- Close, then begin work under the draw process.

Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor and prepares itemized scopes and bids for both Standard and Limited projects. Whoever you hire, choose a contractor who has worked inside the program, because the process rewards contractors who price against the write-up and document completed work for every draw.

faqs.q: What is the maximum for a Limited 203(k)?
faqs.a: The Limited 203(k) covers minor remodeling and nonstructural repairs with total rehabilitation costs up to $75,000. For projects over $15,000, an inspection is required, and for projects of $15,000 or less, the lender may decide whether an inspection is needed. Projects with rehabilitation costs above the $75,000 limit, or that involve structural work, use the Standard 203(k), subject to FHA mortgage limits and other program requirements.

An FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant is required on every Standard 203(k). On a Limited 203(k), a consultant is optional, although the lender may require one. The consultant inspects the property, prepares the write-up of required and requested work with a cost estimate, reviews contractor bids, inspects work before draws are released and documents change orders. Even when optional, some borrowers choose a consultant on older homes or larger Limited projects.

faqs.q: What is the minimum repair cost for a Standard 203(k)?
faqs.a: Rehabilitation costs on a Standard 203(k) must total at least $5,000. The Standard version is designed for major rehabilitation, structural work, additions and complex projects, and it can also be used when rehabilitation costs exceed the $75,000 Limited 203(k) cap, subject to applicable FHA mortgage limits and other program requirements. An FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant is required. The consultant's write-up becomes the scope contractors bid against and the basis for every draw inspection.

faqs.q: Can I do the work myself on a 203(k) loan?
faqs.a: Most lenders do not allow buyers to perform the renovations themselves. The program expects work to be completed by qualified contractors who submit itemized bids, are paid through the draw process and complete work that can be inspected against the agreed scope. If you have construction experience and want to do some of the work, ask your lender directly, but plan on hiring contractors for the project.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) loan on a duplex or fourplex?
faqs.a: Yes. FHA 203(k) loans can be used on eligible two- to four-unit properties, provided the borrower occupies one of the units. Either the Limited or Standard version may apply depending on the work and the rehabilitation cost, and certain conversions of one- to four-unit properties are eligible under the Standard 203(k). The program is not available to investors who will not live in the property.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan pay for a swimming pool?
faqs.a: Pool repairs are eligible, but new pools are not. Luxury additions such as new pools, spas and outdoor kitchens are excluded from the program. The 203(k) is meant to fund improvements to the livability, safety, efficiency and value of the home, such as roofs, systems, kitchens, baths, flooring, windows, accessibility and structural repairs. If an existing pool on the property needs repair, discuss with your lender how that work fits the program before the scope is finalized.
